power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The role of social media in misinformation consumption remains contested.
This disagreement might arise from the failure to distinguish incidental exposure to misinformation from deliberate consumption.
We address this gap by analyzing incoming traffic data, collected in November 2020, to more than 2,000 websites that vary in misinformation and type of bias (liberal, conservative, and conspiracy).

We compare the traffic modalities through which users reach those sites: direct traffic, such as typing a URL or using a bookmark (mostly associated with self-directed information seeking); social traffic, from links clicked on social media; and search traffic, from search engines (mostly associated with incidental exposure).

We found that reliable, low-misinformation websites are reached mainly via search traffic, whereas unreliable ones are mostly reached via direct traffic; this pattern is stronger for conspiracy websites.
Breaking down social traffic by platform reveals that Facebook was the main driver of traffic towards unreliable websites, mostly towards politically biased and entry-level conspiracy websites.

These findings suggest that structural interventions such as algorithmic adjustments and content moderation may reduce incidental exposure among users with low belief commitment, but are unlikely to deter highly committed information seekers, who require targeted, ideologically informed strategies.
Misinformation undermines citizens' ability to make informed decisions, posing a significant threat to democratic processes [1, 2].
text.formatted: Misinformation undermines citizens' ability to make informed decisions, posing a significant threat to democratic processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Among the drivers of its diffusion, social media have often been blamed [3, 4].
text.formatted: Among the drivers of its diffusion, social media have often been blamed <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: Features such as algorithmic curation (e.g., YouTube's ranked recommendations) and platform designs that favor like-minded communities (e.g., Facebook groups) can reinforce users' existing beliefs while filtering out contradictory information, facilitating the spread of misinformation [5] [6] [7] [8].
text.formatted: Features such as algorithmic curation (e.g., YouTube's ranked recommendations) and platform designs that favor like-minded communities (e.g., Facebook groups) can reinforce users' existing beliefs while filtering out contradictory information, facilitating the spread of misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Combined with deeper engagement in echo chambers, this can draw users into "rabbit holes" [9, 10] that amplify extreme viewpoints [11] and reinforce ideological segregation and polarization [12, 13].
text.formatted: Combined with deeper engagement in echo chambers, this can draw users into "rabbit holes" <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref> that amplify extreme viewpoints <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> and reinforce ideological segregation and polarization <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: There is an active debate about how pervasive misinformation actually is in the digital information landscape [14, 15] and whether exposure to misinformation does [16, 17] or does not [18, 19] translate into active engagement, belief uptake, and behavioral change.
text.formatted: There is an active debate about how pervasive misinformation actually is in the digital information landscape <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref> and whether exposure to misinformation does <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref> or does not <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19]</ref> translate into active engagement, belief uptake, and behavioral change.

text.text: But social media can also function as intermediaries [20] whose influence depends on users' predispositions, cognitive biases, and environment [21] [22] [23].
text.formatted: But social media can also function as intermediaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> whose influence depends on users' predispositions, cognitive biases, and environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: For instance, in autocracies and emerging democracies, social media use can be beneficial, increasing political participation and information consumption, whereas in established democracies it can be detrimental, associated with declining political trust, populism, and polarization [24].
text.formatted: For instance, in autocracies and emerging democracies, social media use can be beneficial, increasing political participation and information consumption, whereas in established democracies it can be detrimental, associated with declining political trust, populism, and polarization <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: A critical point concerns the distinction between exposure and consumption.
Because much social media content is processed only superficially [25], researchers have moved beyond mere exposure, analyzing patterns of active consumption such as web browsing activity [26].
text.formatted: Because much social media content is processed only superficially <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>, researchers have moved beyond mere exposure, analyzing patterns of active consumption such as web browsing activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: However, browsing data have their own limitations.
Most tracking tools do not capture in-platform actions, making it difficult to determine whether a visit originated from social media or via other routes [27] (but see [28]).
text.formatted: Most tracking tools do not capture in-platform actions, making it difficult to determine whether a visit originated from social media or via other routes <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> (but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>).

text.text: Moreover, such data are difficult to collect from users with extreme ideologies, who are often mistrustful of research institutions [29].
text.formatted: Moreover, such data are difficult to collect from users with extreme ideologies, who are often mistrustful of research institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: These gaps can be addressed by shifting the focus from individual browsing behavior to website-level incoming traffic patterns.

Rather than following individuals across the web, this approach decomposes a website's incoming traffic into the traffic modalities through which its visits arrive, such as search traffic (from search engines), social traffic (from links clicked on social media), or direct traffic (typing a URL or using a bookmark), among others.

Traffic is aggregated over a website's entire audience rather than over a recruited panel, so it also captures visits from users unwilling to be tracked, such as those most likely to consume extreme content.

Because -in principle-a website's content attracts users seeking that content, systematic differences in traffic modality between types of websites are informative about the information-seeking behavior patterns of the users who reach them.

An earlier analysis of incoming traffic data from 91 websites [30] showed that conspiracy websites were accessed primarily via direct traffic (58% of visits), compared with 18% referred by social media and 14% arriving from search engines.
text.formatted: An earlier analysis of incoming traffic data from 91 websites <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> showed that conspiracy websites were accessed primarily via direct traffic (58% of visits), compared with 18% referred by social media and 14% arriving from search engines.

text.text: In contrast, pro-science and least-biased websites showed the opposite pattern: they were accessed predominantly via search engines (71% of visits), had little direct traffic (13%), and even less social traffic (5%).
A partial replication analyzing 56 Italian misinformation websites found that websites' unreliability correlated negatively with search traffic and positively with direct traffic [31].
text.formatted: A partial replication analyzing 56 Italian misinformation websites found that websites' unreliability correlated negatively with search traffic and positively with direct traffic <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: These analyses suggest that website characteristics are associated with specific patterns of information seeking: reliable websites tend to be reached via search engines, whereas unreliable websites are more often reached via direct traffic.
Yet, given their exploratory nature, limited sample sizes, and lack of key control variables (e.g., website popularity), conclusions drawn from these studies remain tentative.

The studies fail to account for differences between misinformation types (e.g., conspiracy vs politically biased) and social media platforms (e.g., Facebook vs Reddit), and do not offer a comprehensive, comparative analysis of the contribution of each traffic modality.
Here, we analyze patterns of incoming traffic for a large set of websites that vary in unreliability and in the type and strength of their bias.

We first characterize how traffic modality varies with website unreliability, and whether this relationship differs between politically biased and conspiracy websites; we then break down social traffic by social media platforms to assess the contribution of each.
Second, we compare traffic modalities with each other and within each website group.

This comparison informs about the relative contribution of self-directed information seeking (mostly reflected in direct traffic), incidental exposure (mostly reflected in search traffic), and the role of social media as intermediaries (social traffic).

In November 2020, we manually compiled a list of websites (N = 2,734) by surveying the entire content of MediaBiasFactCheck (MBFC, http://www.mediabiasfactcheck.com), a widely used ground-truth dataset in misinformation research (see e.g., [12, 30]).

text.text: For most websites (98.39%, N = 2,690), we mapped their editorial tendency to deliver misinformation using the reliability score developed by Lin et al. [32].
text.formatted: For most websites (98.39%, N = 2,690), we mapped their editorial tendency to deliver misinformation using the reliability score developed by Lin et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: This score was compiled for 11,520 websites by aggregating ratings from six independent expert sources-including professional fact-checkers, MBFC, and NewsGuard (one of the most widely used and comprehensive databases for website trustworthiness ratings [33])-each of which rated websites on dimensions such as trust, reliability, bias, credibility, and transparency.
text.formatted: This score was compiled for 11,520 websites by aggregating ratings from six independent expert sources-including professional fact-checkers, MBFC, and NewsGuard (one of the most widely used and comprehensive databases for website trustworthiness ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>)-each of which rated websites on dimensions such as trust, reliability, bias, credibility, and transparency.

text.text: Scores range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating more reliable websites, and show high correspondence with other indices of website quality, which are themselves highly correlated with one another.

To keep its polarity commensurate with our other website indicators-MBFC bias strength, for which higher values indicate more extreme political or conspiratorial content-we inverted this score (1 -reliability) to obtain a measure of unreliability.

Higher values thus consistently indicate more problematic websites across all indicators (e.g., nasa.gov = .043; infowars.com = .954), and positive slopes indicate traffic that increases with misinformation.
We use MBFC categories to differentiate websites by their bias, in order to investigate differences across groups of unreliable websites.

According to MBFC's descriptions, Politically biased websites (N = 1826 in our sample) are moderately to strongly biased toward either liberal (N = 913; e.g., dailykos.com) or conservative (N = 913; e.g., breitbart.com) ideologies, often reflected in topic selection and use of emotionally charged language.
These websites may publish misleading reports or omit ideologically unfavorable information, and some of these websites are considered less trustworthy.

Conspiracy websites (N = 294; e.g., infowars.com) frequently publish unverifiable claims tied to conspiracy theories and often lack credible evidence and are generally unreliable for factual information.
Finally, our sample includes minimally biased (MB) websites (e.g., reuters.com), which are those labelled by MBFC as pro-science and least-biased (N = 614 in our sample).
These websites remain committed to scientific integrity, avoid emotionally charged or misleading language, and are considered among the most credible media outlets.

Although our focus is on biased websites that vary in unreliability, we retain minimally biased websites whenever a full spectrum of unreliability is needed or when specific ideological biases are irrelevant.

MBFC provides coarse-grained bias-strength ratings for each category (e.g., the degree of conspiratorial content on a 1-5 scale), which are highly correlated with unreliability (r2688 = .84, p < .001; expectedly because MBFC is one of the indices used to compute the unreliability score).
text.formatted: MBFC provides coarse-grained bias-strength ratings for each category (e.g., the degree of conspiratorial content on a 1-5 scale), which are highly correlated with unreliability (r2688 = .84, p < .001; expectedly because MBFC is one of the indices used to compute the unreliability score).

text.text: Throughout, we refer to MBFC's five labels (pro-science, least-biased, liberal, conservative, and conspiracy) as categories, to the groupings used in our models (liberal, conservative, conspiracy, and minimally biased) as groups, and to each combination of category and bias strength (e.g., CT01, R05) as a bias level.
We refer to conspiracy websites with the lowest bias strength (CT01-CT02) as entry-level conspiracy websites.

Note that website group and unreliability are measured independently: group membership reflects MBFC's categorical classification of content, whereas unreliability is a continuous score aggregated across six expert sources [32].

text.text: As a result, unreliability varies within each group.
For example, conspiracy websites are on average less reliable than minimally biased ones, but the two distributions overlap.
A description of MBFC categories and unreliability is given in the Supplemental Material (SM; Appendix SM1).

text.text: As in previous work [30, 31], we focus on three primary traffic modalities through which users access websites, namely search, direct, and social traffic.

text.text: Search traffic is the percentage of total visits originating from search engine queries.

Search traffic has been associated with greater source diversity in web-tracking data: users who reach news through search engines visit a more ideologically diverse set of outlets, including outlets that do not match their political preferences [35], and have more varied news diets and higher overall news exposure [20]; moreover, search engines direct users to a more diverse set of sources than social media do [36].

text.text: Direct traffic is the percentage of total visits that SimilarWeb attributes to no referring source, that is, visits in which users type the URL into their browser or use a bookmark.

It is therefore commonly taken to reflect self-directed, preference-driven information selection: studies using web-tracking data have linked direct traffic to more congenial, ideologically aligned engagement [35].

text.text: SimilarWeb breaks down social traffic by platform.

Here, we collected traffic from Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, and Reddit, which together account for approximately 80% of social traffic in our sample (M = 79.92, SD = 15.27, range: 18.21-99.97; these four platforms were chosen for their popularity at the time, confirmed with a reanalysis of 96 websites two years later; see Appendix SM2).

A website's popularity was quantified via total visits, measured by SimilarWeb as the monthly number of visits.

We reasoned that an unpopular website is more likely to be accessed via direct traffic because it is likely to not appear within the first pages of a search engine; therefore, we controlled for popularity to exclude this artifact.

However, note that in our data, total visits did not correlate with direct traffic (r1908 = -.004, p = .875), but correlated positively with search traffic (r1908 = .10, p < .001) and negatively with social traffic (r1907 = -.12, p < .001), which led to its inclusion in all models.

text.text: We analyzed incoming traffic to more than 2,000 websites that differed in unreliability-a proxy for misinformation content-and in the type and strength of their bias.
As website unreliability increased, the shares of direct and social traffic increased, while the share of search traffic declined.

Traffic patterns were broadly similar across website groups, with one notable exception: as unreliability increased, conspiracy websites showed the steepest increase in direct traffic relative to search traffic.
By contrast, the balance between social and search traffic shifted toward social traffic for politically biased websites, but not for conspiracy websites.
Among the social media platforms examined, Facebook traffic was most strongly associated with website unreliability.
This association differed by website group: it was positive for politically biased websites but not significant for conspiracy websites.
Twitter, YouTube, and Reddit each accounted for a smaller share of incoming traffic than Facebook, on average.
The most consistent pattern across our results was a decline in search traffic with unreliability.
This decline, however, does not necessarily mean that search engines actively prioritize reliable sources.
Search rankings rely in part on links among websites, which carry information about popularity and, by extension, about the consensus on a website's credibility.
Consistent with this, unreliability correlated negatively with total visits, and total visits correlated positively, albeit weakly, with search traffic (see Appendix SM4).

Because our data are observational and aggregated at the website level, the association between unreliability and search traffic may therefore partly be a by-product of web interconnectivity and popularity, rather than evidence that search engines assess credibility directly.
Direct traffic exceeds social traffic, particularly for websites with the greatest bias.

Direct traffic, which includes also bookmarking favorite websites, was associated with greater engagement than search and social traffic, as reflected in longer visits, more pages viewed per session, and lower bounce rates.

Such patterns are consistent with more self-directed, preference-driven visits, but note that our observational data cannot allow us to distinguish the preference for belief-congruent information from other forms of self-directed information seeking (more on this later).
Selective exposure has been linked to stronger motivation [37], which may be particularly relevant when beliefs are closely tied to identity and worldviews [38].

text.text: Note that search and social traffic should not automatically be treated as incidental: these modalities can also include self-directed information seeking.
Search traffic, for example, is not always informational: people may search for a topic without a preferred destination.
Approximately 10% of Google queries are navigational, meaning that users are seeking a specific website or page (e.g., "covid symptoms wiki" vs "covid symptoms"; see [45]).

text.text: Thus, particularly for highly committed information seekers, some search visits may be self-directed and may resemble direct visits in this respect.
If anything, direct traffic may underestimate the extent of self-directed information seeking.

Similarly, social traffic can arise in different contexts, such as links shared in ideologically aligned communities (e.g., Facebook groups), algorithmic recommendations (e.g., YouTube videos suggested on the basis of viewing histories), or posts from acquaintances.

Although both algorithmic ranking and engagement-based distribution on social media can reinforce ideological clustering and echo chambers [12, 13], they might be involving different degrees of self-directed selection.

text.text: Clicks from within a chosen, like-minded community may reflect selective exposure, whereas links encountered in broader feeds may be more incidental.
Unfortunately, our data cannot distinguish between these contexts.
Selection may also operate before the click: users' browsing histories can shape algorithmic recommendations, and their choice of communities may itself reflect selective exposure [48, 49].

text.text: Our results are consistent with behavioral patterns of commitment-driven information seeking.
In the following, we provide a tentative explanation for the underlying psychological mechanisms.
The increase in direct (over search) traffic with unreliability was strongest for conspiracy websites.
This pattern is consistent with a commitment-driven account of information seeking, in which initial exposure can be incidental but may gradually become more systematic as belief commitment deepens.

A person may first encounter a conspiratorial claim through a social media feed or by searching for a specific concern, such as whether COVID-19 statistics are exaggerated, without yet being strongly committed to conspiratorial thinking.
At this stage, a link to an entry-level conspiracy website may appear relevant and compelling, and a single search or click can trigger a broader process of information gathering.

As more "evidence" accumulates, an initial incidental encounter can build into a more coherent narrative that "something is wrong with COVID", and the person may then move across an interconnected system of webpages that reinforce the same worldview.

Entry-level conspiracy websites can therefore function as entry points to deeper conspiratorial engagement, reinforcing belief systems and potentially drawing users into "rabbit holes" of conspiracy theories [9, 10].

text.text: As belief commitment strengthens, users may increasingly bypass intermediaries and engage in more self-directed information seeking.

This shift from social to direct traffic along the unreliability continuum may resemble the solitary "epistemic journey" and "spiritual awakening" characterizing conspiracy believers [29, 53], who often present themselves as independent reasoners and portray their research as autonomous [54].

text.text: However, this pattern should not be interpreted as evidence that believers are less susceptible to social influence.
On the contrary, it suggests that once belief commitment is established, information seeking becomes less dependent on external intermediaries and more self-directed.
This interpretation is consistent with evidence that social influence remains relevant even when users increasingly seek information on their own [54].

text.text: Our findings also show distinct differences in how social media platforms route traffic to unreliable websites.

Facebook emerged as the platform delivering the largest share of social traffic to unreliable websites, aligning with evidence that its engagement-driven ranking algorithms and group-based ecosystem foster ideological homogeneity and misinformation amplification [12].

text.text: However, as websites' unreliability increased so did the share of Facebook traffic towards politically biased, but not conspiracy websites.

One tentative explanation is that temporary efforts by Facebook to reduce the spread of misinformation around the 2020 election may have disproportionately limited referrals to the most unreliable websites starting already with A/B testing in the summer of 2020 [55].

text.text: These measures, however, were not specific to conspiracy websites and our data cannot establish whether they explain this pattern.
YouTube contributed less to overall traffic towards unreliable websites: we found that link only for conservative websites.
This seems in contrast with evidence for its role in self-driven radicalization and to dissemination of conspiracy theories and extreme content [56].

Twitter was more strongly associated with traffic towards politically biased websites than with conspiracy websites, consistent with studies indicating that its fact-checking interventions (at least in 2020) reduced prolonged exposure to conspiracy theories [57], although misinformation persists [58].

Unlike algorithmically curated platforms such as Facebook and YouTube, Reddit's voting mechanism enables collective content regulation, reducing misinformation visibility [60].

text.text: Our data were collected in November 2020.
Since then, the online information landscape has changed.

Although we demonstrate that traffic patterns remained relatively stable over a two-year period, changes in website and social media ownership, misinformation policies, and editorial practices [33] can lead to changes in misinformation dissemination and traffic modalities.

text.text: Finally, a cautionary note is warranted.
Our results should not be interpreted as downplaying the role of social media in the dissemination of misinformation.

Although this study focused on assessing the extent to which social media drive traffic to external websites, it is crucial to recognize that misinformation can also cause harm within social media platforms themselves, without redirecting users to external websites (e.g., YouTube).
The absence of website clicks from social media posts does not necessarily imply a lack of exposure to misinformation.
Unfortunately, this type of data cannot capture the consumption of misinformation that occurs entirely within social media ecosystems.
Capturing such exposure would require browsing data or platform-specific social media data.
Our analysis of incoming traffic across a large sample of websites with varying degrees of unreliability and bias reveals two distinct patterns in misinformation consumption.

While incidental exposure, mostly via search traffic, introduces users with low belief commitment to unreliable content, self-directed information seeking appears to drive consumption of websites with the highest bias strength, particularly conspiracy websites.

Our interpretation is that unlike politically biased websites, which rely more on social traffic, consumption of conspiracy content tends to follow solitary epistemic journeys, where individuals rely less on social media and more on self-reinforcing discovery mechanisms.
Our results carry important implications for intervention strategies.

While structural interventions such as content moderation and deplatforming may help limit incidental exposure to misinformation, they are unlikely to deter users with conspiratorial worldviews, who often migrate to alternative platforms [63] or perceive moderation efforts as censorship, further reinforcing their worldview [17].
text.formatted: While structural interventions such as content moderation and deplatforming may help limit incidental exposure to misinformation, they are unlikely to deter users with conspiratorial worldviews, who often migrate to alternative platforms <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[63]</ref> or perceive moderation efforts as censorship, further reinforcing their worldview <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the growing reluctance of major platforms to implement misinformation countermeasures raises concerns about the longterm sustainability of structural interventions [1].
text.formatted: Additionally, the growing reluctance of major platforms to implement misinformation countermeasures raises concerns about the longterm sustainability of structural interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Given these challenges, individual-level approaches, including psychological inoculation, emerge as more viable solutions, with large-scale prebunking initiatives holding promise as scalable interventions [64].

text.text: Ultimately, while no single approach can fully counter misinformation, a comprehensive strategy that assesses costs and benefits while integrating targeted platform policies with prebunking campaigns offers the most effective path forward in mitigating the societal impact of misinformation in both the short and long term.

text.text: At the time of compilation, MBFC contained approximately 3,000 annotated websites, primarily news outlets; as of January 2025, this figure has grown to over 8,900.
For politically biased and conspiracy websites, MBFC provides bias strength ratings.

Bias strength for political websites is rated on a 3-point scale (1 = center right|left,2 = right|left, and3 = extreme right|left).

To facilitate direct comparison with the conspiracy-bias scale, we rescaled political-bias ratings onto the same 5-point-range metric by remapping the three original categories (to 1, 3, and 5, respectively).

Figure S4 presents the mean weighted proportion of each traffic modality (direct, search, and social; top panels), as well as the breakdown of social traffic by platform (Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, and Reddit; bottom panels).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">S4</ref> presents the mean weighted proportion of each traffic modality (direct, search, and social; top panels), as well as the breakdown of social traffic by platform (Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, and Reddit; bottom panels).

text.text: These proportions are shown for all websites (Panels A, D), by website category (Panels B, E), and by bias level (Panels C, F).
Panel A shows that search and direct traffic were the primary traffic modalities for all websites, while social traffic accounted for a relatively small proportion (8.42%).
Panel B reveals an increasing trend in both social and direct traffic from pro-science to conspiracy websites.
Specifically, social traffic increased from 2.89% in pro-science websites to 14.65% in conspiracy websites.
Similarly, direct traffic rose from 19.84% in pro-science websites to 48.72% in conspiracy websites.
Panel C indicates that social traffic was highest for entry-level conspiracy websites (CT01: 23.55%), followed by conservative websites with the highest bias strength (R05: 17.78%).
Direct traffic accounted for approximately or above 70% of total visits in websites with the highest bias strength, including L05 (71.60%), R05 (60.69%), CT04 (74.35%), and CT05 (69.05%).
These findings support the idea that websites with the highest bias strength are primarily accessed via direct traffic.
Among social media platforms, Panel D shows that Facebook delivered the largest share of social traffic overall (39.28%), followed by Twitter (23.57%), Reddit (15.47%), and YouTube (13.91%).
Facebook delivered the largest share of social traffic to conservative websites, accounting for 44.80% of their total social traffic (Panel E).
However, Facebook traffic was disproportionately high for entry-level conspiracy websites, contributing 60.93% of traffic for bias level CT02 (see Panel F).
In contrast, Reddit delivered the largest share of social traffic to pro-science websites (23.76%).
Notably, 23.59% of social traffic to CT01 originated from platforms other than the four mainstream social media platforms analyzed in this study.
